title: Did Ptolemy observe the Almagest star catalogue or adapt Hipparchus's?
short: Ptolemy's catalogue of about 1,025 stars claims his own observations; statistical anomalies suggest much of it derives from Hipparchus three centuries earlier.
matters: The Almagest catalogue is the oldest fully preserved star catalogue and the basis of Western and Islamic stellar astronomy until Ulugh Beg. Whether it records new observations bears on Ptolemy's reliability as a witness to his own practice, on the reconstruction of Hipparchus's lost catalogue, on the value of ancient positions for measuring precession and proper motion, and on broader arguments about how ancient scientists used data.
stuck: Ptolemy dates the catalogue to the first year of Antoninus (AD 137) and implies he observed it, but its longitudes are systematically about 1° too small for that date, consistent with adding a precession of 1° per century to positions for Hipparchus's epoch. Statistical tests of epoch, observer latitude, rounding patterns and error structure have yielded conflicting verdicts because the catalogue may mix sources and because results depend on modelling choices. Until 2022 there were almost no direct Hipparchan coordinates against which to compare.
solved: Recovery of enough of Hipparchus's own coordinates (from palimpsests or other witnesses) to show for a substantial sample of stars whether Ptolemy's entries equal Hipparchan values shifted by 2°40′ in longitude, or differ in ways that require independent measurement; or a pre-registered statistical analysis of the whole catalogue, using modern astrometry, that discriminates between the two hypotheses for defined subsets of stars.
approach: The statistical case has been argued many times, from Vogt (1925) and Newton (1977) through Evans (1987), Graßhoff (1990), Shevchenko (1990) and Dambis and Efremov (2000), with Duke (2002) questioning whether proper motions can separate the two epochs at all. Verbunt and van Gent (2012) already provide a machine-readable catalogue, and Toomer (1984) the standard translation, so teams need not start from the text.

Rebuild the competing tests on one shared footing: a single edition of the catalogue, with variants from Greek witnesses such as Vat. gr. 1594 and the Arabic and Latin tradition inventoried by Ptolemaeus Arabus et Latinus, matched star by star to modern positions from Hipparcos and Gaia DR3, described by Vallenari (2023) for the Gaia Collaboration. The identification of each ancient star with a modern one is the decision that most shapes the data, and doubtful identifications should be flagged rather than silently resolved.

With every assumption explicit, the main hypotheses can be tested side by side: that Ptolemy observed with a miscalibrated instrument, as Evans (1987) proposed; that he adapted Hipparchan coordinates by adding precession; or that the catalogue is a mixture. Reporting results by constellation, magnitude and source subset would show whether different parts of the catalogue have different origins.

The Hipparchan coordinates recovered by Gysembergh, Williams and Zingg (2022) from the Codex Climaci Rescriptus give, for the first time, a direct sample to compare with Ptolemy's entries. Even a few dozen stars, compared after converting between Hipparchus's equatorial and Ptolemy's ecliptic systems, would test the copying hypothesis more directly than error statistics can.

For much of the catalogue the answer is likely to remain probabilistic, with some regions attributable to Hipparchus and others uncertain. Historians of astronomy and astronomers should review both the star identifications and the modelling of proper motion and refraction.

Further direct evidence depends on multispectral imaging of the remaining undertext of the Codex Climaci Rescriptus and other Sinai palimpsests by imaging scientists, and on the Museum of the Bible, St Catherine's Monastery and partner libraries continuing to open these manuscripts to study.

existing.title: Versuch einer Wiederherstellung von Hipparchs Fixsternverzeichnis
existing.note: Reconstructed Hipparchan coordinates from the Commentary on Aratus and found that many of Ptolemy's entries could not be simple copies of them.

existing.title: The Crime of Claudius Ptolemy
existing.note: Charged Ptolemy with fabricating observations, including deriving the star catalogue from Hipparchus.

existing.title: Ptolemy's Almagest
existing.note: Standard English translation with the full catalogue, used as the textual basis for most modern analyses.

existing.title: On the Origin of the Ptolemaic Star Catalogue (Parts 1 and 2)
existing.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy 18 (3): 155–172; 18 (4): 233–278
existing.note: Argued that Ptolemy did observe, using an instrument calibrated with a faulty solar theory, which would explain the systematic longitude error.

existing.title: The History of Ptolemy's Star Catalogue
existing.note: Statistical study concluding that the catalogue rests substantially on Hipparchan data adjusted by Ptolemy, while rejecting simple fraud.

existing.title: An Analysis of Errors in the Star Catalogues of Ptolemy and Ulugh Beg
existing.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy 21 (2): 187–201
existing.note: Compared error structures across catalogues and argued for a Hipparchan origin of much of Ptolemy's data.

existing.authors: A. K. Dambis and Yu. N. Efremov
existing.title: Dating Ptolemy's Star Catalogue through Proper Motions: The Hipparchan Epoch
existing.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy 31 (2): 115–134
existing.note: Used fast-moving stars to date the observations to roughly the second century BC, consistent with Hipparchus rather than Ptolemy.

existing.title: Dating the Almagest Star Catalogue Using Proper Motions: A Reconsideration
existing.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy 33 (1): 45–55
existing.note: Argued that proper-motion dating cannot statistically distinguish Hipparchus's epoch from Ptolemy's.

existing.title: The Epoch of the Constellations on the Farnese Atlas and Their Origin in Hipparchus's Lost Catalogue
existing.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy 36 (2): 167–196
existing.note: Dated the Farnese Atlas globe to about 125 BC and linked it to Hipparchus's catalogue; the identification has been contested.

existing.title: A Survey of the Almagest
existing.note: Standard guide to the Almagest, with Jones's revision summarizing the catalogue debate.

existing.authors: F. Verbunt and R. H. van Gent
existing.title: The Star Catalogues of Ptolemaios and Ulugh Beg
existing.note: Published machine-readable catalogues and found that the error pattern supports Hipparchan origin for most entries.

existing.authors: Victor Gysembergh, Peter J. Williams and Emanuel Zingg
existing.title: New Evidence for Hipparchus' Star Catalogue Revealed by Multispectral Imaging
existing.venue: Journal for the History of Astronomy 53 (4): 383–393
existing.note: Recovered Hipparchan equatorial coordinates for stars of Corona Borealis from the undertext of the Codex Climaci Rescriptus, the first direct sample of his catalogue.

existing.title: Gaia Data Release 3: Summary of the Content and Survey Properties
existing.note: Current high-precision astrometry and proper motions for back-computing ancient star positions.

archives.repository: Museum of the Bible, Washington, DC
archives.collection: Codex Climaci Rescriptus (Green Collection), Syriac palimpsest with Greek astronomical undertext
archives.note: Holds most leaves of the palimpsest that yielded Hipparchan coordinates; multispectral images have been made for part of the codex.

holdings.name: Codex Climaci Rescriptus (Syriac palimpsest, Green Collection)
holdings.note: Most of its 146 leaves are here; the Greek undertext on folios 47-54 and 64 includes the Aratus material and the Hipparchan star coordinates recovered in 2022.

archives.repository: UCLA Library and St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai
archives.collection: Sinai Palimpsests Project (multispectral images of palimpsests from St Catherine's)
archives.note: Open-access multispectral images of Sinai palimpsests, among which further Greek scientific undertexts may survive; free registration required.

archives.collection: Vat. gr. 1594 (ninth-century Almagest) and other Greek Almagest manuscripts
archives.note: One of the oldest complete Greek witnesses of the catalogue, fully digitized on DigiVatLib.

holdings.name: Vat. gr. 1594 (Heiberg's B)
holdings.note: Ninth-century Almagest with Theon's prolegomena and two layers of scholia, one of the oldest Greek witnesses to the catalogue text.

holdings.name: Vat. gr. 180 (Heiberg's D)
holdings.note: Tenth-century Almagest carrying essentially the same scholia as Vat. gr. 1594 and Marc. gr. 313, a further witness for the catalogue text.

archives.collection: Ptolemaeus Arabus et Latinus (database of Arabic and Latin Ptolemaic manuscripts)
archives.note: Inventory of Arabic and Latin witnesses of the Almagest, whose catalogue variants help establish the text's original values.
Modern astrometry with proper motions used to compute where each star stood in 130 BC and AD 137.

holdings.name: The Hipparcos and Tycho Catalogues (ESA 1997)
holdings.note: Machine-readable positions, proper motions and photometry of 118,000 Hipparcos stars (Hipparcos main catalogue) for computing star positions at Hipparchan and Ptolemaic epochs.
